title: Balancing efficiency and fairness in liver transplant access: tradeoff curves for the assessment of organ distribution policies
contribution: Parameterizes the three OPTN liver distribution frameworks (acuity circles, optimized districts, a continuous score MELD − λ·distance), simulates each setting in SRTR's LSAM and plots deaths and the SD of median MELD at transplant against transport distance; at matched distance the continuous score saves 104 deaths a year against the current 11-region policy and gives the best curves, and OPOM-based urgency adds about 500.
problem_entry: {AP+DA; IO only in the unread SDC} Geographic disparity in liver access persisted two decades after the 1998 Final Rule; a 2018 lawsuit and DHHS's request for a policy without DSAs or regions met three OPTN frameworks with no consensus, so the paper compares them all on efficiency–fairness tradeoff curves (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Index each distribution concept by its parameters (circle radii and MELD bands; number and grouping of districts; λ in MELD − λ·distance), sweep them through LSAM, and compare each reference policy with the continuous-score policy whose λ matches its average transport distance (pp. 2–4; Table 1, p. 4).
assumptions: LSAM 2014 on SRTR data 2007–2011, 20 runs for each of 2010 and 2011; outcomes: deaths, transplants, MMaT and σMMaT across 58 DSAs, group disparities, distances and share flown; urgency by MELD, MELD-Na or OPOM (p. 3). Admitted: LSAM may overestimate deaths averted and cannot model changed listing or acceptance behaviour; only a linear distance term is tried (p. 7).
proof_devices: n/a in the article: the optimization behind the optimized districts and the policy parameter grids is in the Supplemental Digital Content (pp. 2–3), not in the file and not read
matched-cost comparison: λ chosen so that the continuous score's average transport distance equals each reference policy's (Table 1, p. 4)
experiments: 11-region policy: 2,510 deaths a year at 244.7 nm; matched CS (λ = 0.022): 2,406, −104 (one-SD interval −140 to −68), σMMaT −29.8%; against AC 250/500 −30 (−53, −7); against AC 300/600 −24 (−58, 10), an interval through zero [my reading] (Table 1, p. 4). OPOM instead of MELD: about 500 fewer deaths a year, 556 with CS (pp. 6–7). Rounding distance to 10–50 nm barely changes outcomes (pp. 4–5). Marginal-graft discards trend up with distance (Table 2, p. 6); [my reading] at matched distance CS discards more donor-over-70 grafts than the current policy (31.7% against 28.7%).
positioning: Applies the authors' efficiency–fairness tradeoff framework (Bertsimas, Farias, Trichakis 2012, ref. 7) and OPOM (ref. 10) to the three OPTN frameworks; says the approved acuity-circle policy is 'by no means' mathematically optimized; cites Snyder et al. for nonlinear continuous scores (pp. 2, 6–7).
writing: Clinical-journal format (structured abstract); the results rest on two tradeoff figures and one matched-distance table; the close claims 'superiority to all other policies' (p. 7).
limits_future: Stated: LSAM overestimation and fixed behaviour; one linear implementation (p. 7). Future: continuous distribution for all solid organs; curves for other metrics (pp. 1, 7). Not stated [my reading]: the AC 300/600 comparison's interval includes zero.

method_links.note: Fairness and efficiency priced on curves indexed by one interpretable knob (λ, score per nautical mile), with the single policy left to the transplant community. No solution-independent bound, and the weakest comparison (interval through zero) is not flagged.

The owner's current rule (11 regions) and its newly approved rule (AC 250/500) are the baselines; fairness is scored on the owner's accepted metric (MMaT, accepted by the OPTN committee in March 2013); the simulator's limits are printed. No field test.

The Trichakis fairness programme reaches a clinical journal; the contribution statement assigns implementation to Papalexopoulos, Trichakis and Wang and problem definition, approach and writing to Bertsimas. The concept returns with UNOS in 2025 (S476, c2-07).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: each reference policy is compared with the continuous-score policy whose λ gives the same average transport distance, so outcome gains are not bought with extra travel

transferable: Tune the new policy family's knob until a cost metric equals the incumbent's (here transport distance), then report outcome differences with intervals (Table 1, p. 4).
Answer a stakeholder objection to a continuous score (two hospitals across town) by coarsening its input (distances rounded to 10–50 nm) and showing outcomes do not move (pp. 4–5, 7).
Publish the whole frontier as an interactive site so others can examine metric pairs the paper does not plot (p. 6).
coauthors: Theodore Papalexopoulos, Nikolaos Trichakis, Yuchen Wang, Ryutaro Hirose, Parsia A. Vagefi

quotes.text: Continuous scoring policies dominated all others considered and allowed for the greatest reduction of deaths across all transport distances.

Limitations of this study include that estimating number of deaths averted using LSAM may represent an overestimation, and that LSAM cannot account for changes in practitioner listing or acceptance behavior

title: Bus routing optimization helps Boston public schools design better policies
contribution: Reports the MIT–BPS collaboration: the BiRD decomposition has routed Boston's school buses since 2017 (50 fewer buses, 7%, an estimated $5 million, after BPS added buses back), and a GQAP start-time model gave the district trade-off curves and a plan (high-school starts before 8:00 from 74% to 6%, $12 million reinvested) that was not implemented after opposition to changing 85% of schools' times.
problem_entry: {AP+IO; HS} BPS spent $120 million (about 10% of its budget) on transport in 2017, growing 5–7% a year; routes were drafted by hand in about 3,000 people-hours, so no policy could be costed; vendors had no tool, so BPS ran a 60-day crowdsourced challenge that the MIT team won (pp. 4–5).
key_idea: BiRD: IO stop assignment, insertion trips joined by set cover, several Pareto scenarios per school (buses against ride time), one per school chosen by a network-flow IO, then IO bus scheduling (pp. 6–7); start times as a GQAP with routing-affinity costs, solved by local improvement over random subsets each re-solved by MIO, with policy goals as weighted GQAP-representable terms (pp. 9, 11).
assumptions: Challenge data with approximate addresses, school locations and vetted stops (p. 5); 25,000 riders, 5,000 door-to-door, a heterogeneous fleet of over 700 buses (p. 4); Google Maps car travel times, admitted to misroute large buses (p. 8); a community survey of preferred times (pp. 10–11); GQAP formulations intractable even on small instances, hence local search (p. 9); compatibility-cost parameters by cross-validation (p. 9).
proof_devices: decomposition into IO subproblems bridged by joint scenario selection (Fig. 3, p. 7)
start-time selection as a generalized quadratic assignment problem with single and pairwise affinity costs (pp. 9, 11)
local improvement: re-solve a random subset of schools' times by MIO with the rest fixed; near-optimality of one-school subsets with restarts is cited from the PNAS paper's synthetic tests (p. 9)
experiments: Challenge data: up to 20% fewer buses (p. 7). Deployment 2017: 75 fewer buses (12%) in the plan, 50 (7%) after BPS added buses back, an estimated $5 million and 20,000 pounds of carbon emissions a day; first-week on-time performance worse than the year before, better than the prior year by November (p. 8). Start times: 450 against 600 buses on transport alone (pp. 9–10); a satisfaction–cost curve (Fig. 5a, pp. 10–11); the chosen plan cut early high-school starts from 74% to 6% and late elementary dismissals from 33% to 15%, with $12 million reinvested, but changed 85% of schools (median one hour) and was not implemented (pp. 11–12). No gaps or solve times are reported.
positioning: School bus routing as a special case of vehicle routing; prior work optimizes the subproblems in isolation or uses metaheuristics; start-time selection has been studied little (Fügenschuh; Banerjee and Smilowitz) (pp. 5–6, 9).
writing: Practice-journal narrative: district history, the challenge, the method in two pages, deployment with its rough first week, and a frank section headed 'Dramatic Change Prevented Implementation' (pp. 2–12).
limits_future: Stated: car travel times, first-week delays, survey framing and representativeness, loss aversion, after-school plans that were not school-specific; the plan was not implemented (pp. 8, 12). After: a school committee policy with quantifiable objectives, a Boston Globe interactive (p. 12); Dynamic Ideas in talks with almost 30 districts and partnering with 3 (p. 13).

method_links.note: Owner, decision, data and current rule (manual routing, three bell tiers) come first; the deployment report includes the poor first week; the plan not adopted is called not implemented, as the Workflow D checkpoint asks. This is the group's own account of the episode behind Method 5's correction [05 §5.1]: the district saw the curve, but school-level changes surfaced only after the plan was proposed.
Community satisfaction priced in buses and dollars on a trade-off curve, with policy weights as the knob.
The exact GQAP stalls, so local improvement with random restarts is used (Heuristic 3); no gap or certificate is given for the deployed solutions.
A company started by Bertsimas (Dynamic Ideas) carries the method to other districts; one applied write-up per deployment.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the paper lists why the start-time plan failed: the survey did not show options against current times, start times were not mapped to end times, loss aversion, unrepresentative engagement, after-school plans that were not school-specific

transferable: Generate several Pareto scenarios per component (school) instead of one, then pick one per component jointly by IO; this joins single- and multi-component subproblems (pp. 6–7).
When an exact quadratic assignment model is intractable, re-solve a random subset of assignments by MIO with the rest fixed, from several random starts (p. 9).
Report both the algorithmic and the deployed savings, and plan for the operator to add capacity back when inputs may be optimistic (p. 8).
In a stakeholder survey, show each option against the current state and map coupled consequences (start time to end time); the paper names their absence as a cause of failure (p. 12).
coauthors: Arthur Delarue, William Eger, John Hanlon, Sébastien Martin

quotes.text: Each additional point of community satisfaction in Boston costs dozens of additional buses and tens of millions of taxpayer dollars.
Ultimately, the district decided that such an important decision should not be implemented without deeper community engagement, and the new bell times did not become a reality.

title: Stable regression: On the power of optimization over randomization
contribution: Replaces the random training/validation split by a robust problem that trains on the hardest subset of size k, reduced by LP duality to an LP or convex QP; on 10 UCI and two synthetic data sets (1,000 repetitions) it lowers average prediction error and the variability of predictions, coefficients and hyperparameters, most at 50/50 splits and least against cross-validation, improves support recovery, and an optimal tree explains the hardest subpopulation.
problem_entry: {ML+RO; LO and convex QP as engines; IO for support recovery} The random split is standard practice, yet coefficients, supports and hyperparameters change with it, most when data are scarce; the authors know of no work that chooses splits otherwise (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: min over β of max over binary z with Σz = k of Σ z_i|y_i − x_iᵀβ| plus a penalty; z relaxes to its hull and LP duality of the inner maximum yields one LP or QP; the model is robust to every subpopulation of size k, and the hardest set is described by an optimal classification tree (eqs. 1–3, pp. 5–6; pp. 16–17).
assumptions: ℓ1 loss (ℓ2 said to be similar) (p. 7); 10 UCI data sets and two synthetic ones (n = 30,000, p = 1,000; n = 1,000, p = 30,000; 20% nonzero ±1 coefficients) (p. 7; sizes in Table 1, p. 8); 1,000 repetitions with a random 10% test set (p. 7); big-M L0 constraint for support recovery (pp. 13–14); a diabetes data set with over 100,000 observations and a BIDMC emergency-department data set for interpretation (p. 17).
proof_devices: the inner maximum is linear in z, so binary z relaxes to the convex hull {Σz = k, 0 ≤ z ≤ 1} (p. 5)
LP duality of the inner maximum turns the min–max into one LP (Lasso or no penalty) or convex QP (ridge, elastic net) (eq. 3, p. 6); [my reading] the usual sum-of-the-k-largest-residuals form
no statistical theorem; the shrinking gain is explained by the number of possible splits, largest at k = n/2 (p. 21)
experiments: Average MSE gains: 15.12% (50/50) to 1.00% (90/10) without penalty, 10.82% to 0.31% with penalty, 0.75% and 0.43% against 5- and 10-fold CV (Tables 1–2, pp. 8–9); the SDs follow the same pattern (Tables 3–7, pp. 10–13). Support recovery better at every n with s known; with s from CV, randomization leads slightly at small n (Figs. 1–2, pp. 15–16). Trees on the hardest set: 90% and 71% accuracy (pp. 17–18). Run time 2–3 times a random split's at 50/50–70/30, about 1.02–1.03 at 80/20 and 90/10 (Table 8, pp. 20–21). [my reading] 'In all cases' holds for averages, not for every cell (e.g. Computer Hardware, Tables 3 and 7, pp. 10, 13); no solver, version or machine is named (p. 6).
positioning: Extends the 2015 'optimization over randomization' experimental-design paper (p. 2); contrasts Garbade's (1977) stability tests and Duchi–Namkoong's distributionally robust learning, claiming a nonparametric and cheaper LP/QP route (p. 2).
writing: The abstract opens with 'the widely held belief'; every table caption repeats the average gains; the abstract's scaling claim ('essentially any desired size') is backed by sizes up to n = 30,000 or p = 30,000 (pp. 1, 7, 20).
limits_future: Stated: a smaller edge against CV (pp. 1, 21); interpretation examples chosen where experts could check them (p. 19). Future: domains without prior intuition (p. 19). [my reading] Not stated: cells where randomization wins; which optimization column the CV columns are compared with (Table 2, p. 9).

method_links.note: A step owned by statistics (the random split) is written as a robust problem, and LP duality keeps it in the LP/QP class of the nominal regression.

The incumbent (random splits; 5- and 10-fold CV added as 'a fairer comparison') is dueled on real data and on synthetic data with known truth; certificates are moot for LP/QP, but the MIO support-recovery runs report no limit or gap, and no solver or machine is named.
The abstract opens with the field's belief (Heuristic 9), but MIO is called 'nowadays highly solvable' with no figure.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimization over randomization (Taste mark 3 as a Method)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a randomized step of standard practice (the training/validation split) is replaced by an optimization problem; the paper names the 2015 experimental-design paper as the origin of the theme; S357 in this batch does the same for the bootstrap

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: explain the adversary with an interpretable model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an optimal classification tree is fitted with the worst-case (hardest-set) indicator as the label, and its splits are checked with endocrinology and emergency-department experts

transferable: When a procedure picks a subset at random (a split, a sample), write the choice as an inner maximum over z with Σz = k, relax z to its hull and dualize; the problem stays in the nominal class (pp. 5–6).
Fit an optimal classification tree with the worst-case indicator as the label to describe the hardest subpopulation, and check the tree with domain experts (pp. 17–19).
Report stability (SDs over repeated test splits of predictions, coefficients and hyperparameters), not only mean error (Tables 3–7, pp. 9–13).

quotes.text: We investigate and ultimately suggest remediation to the widely held belief that the best way to train regression models is via random assignment of our data to training and validation sets.
When compared to cross-validation, the optimization approach still has an advantage, but it is markedly smaller.

title: Relative robust and adaptive optimization
contribution: Shows that competitive-ratio and regret objectives in robust LO (including affine adaptability) keep the nominal class by duality when the clairvoyant value is concave in the uncertainty, gives a MILO cutting-plane method for the convex case under budget sets, blends competitive ratio and normalized absolute robustness into Pareto-efficient solutions with one knob λ, and tests them on flow, inventory and facility-location problems, where relative solutions often do better on most scenarios at modest extra cost.
problem_entry: {RO; LO and IO as engines} Early robust discrete optimization used relative criteria, but the past decade used the absolute worst case, held to be more tractable; absolute RO can let one bad realization dominate and perform poorly on most scenarios (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: Split by the curvature of the clairvoyant value Π(ξ): concave → substitute, merge the minimizations and dualize (robust LP stays LP, ellipsoid gives SOCP); convex → vertex theorem and exact binary linearization give a MILO inner problem for cutting planes; normalize the absolute objective by ΠRO and blend it with the competitive ratio by λ (pp. 4–9).
assumptions: Offline problem feasible and bounded for every ξ (p. 4); Π(ξ) > 0 for CR (p. 6); finite upper bounds and a budget set in the convex case (p. 7); polyhedral or ellipsoidal sets (p. 4); linear decision rules for recourse (pp. 4, 13, 15); synthetic instances only (pp. 10–17).
proof_devices: substitute the offline LP into the inner problem, merge the two minimizations and take the LP dual (eqs. 12–14, pp. 5–6)
epigraph variable z for the competitive ratio, which keeps convexity since z ≥ 0 (pp. 6)
cutting planes with lazy constraints when the offline problem is a MILO (p. 6)
Theorem 1: a biconvex maximum over polytopes is attained at a pair of vertices, reproduced from the literature (p. 7)
exact linearization of binary × bounded continuous products, checked by enumerating the two binary cases (pp. 7–8)
normalized robust objective fNR = f/ΠRO makes the blend dimensionless; λ = ε picks the best CR solution among RO optima (pp. 8–9)
experiments: JuMP and Gurobi 6.5.0 on an Intel 2.8 GHz Core i7-4960HQ; cuts until no violation exceeds 10⁻³ (p. 10). Layered graph: CR better at the median (13.2 against 15.6) and in relative cost almost everywhere, RO better only at the extreme tail; dense graph roughly the opposite (p. 11). RO 50–100 times the deterministic LP, CR 10–20 times RO, 3.6 s against 0.3 s at n = 50 (p. 11). Inventory: λ from 0 to 1 traces a frontier, each solve under 5 s; λ = 0.6 called an excellent trade-off (pp. 13–14). Facility location: regret reformulation as fast as RO; cutting planes 80 s against 2 s at n = 20, stopped beyond 100 s at n ≥ 25 (pp. 17–18); RO stocks 781 units against 990 and 1,045 and leaves profit on most scenarios (pp. 17–19).
positioning: Revives the relative criteria of Kouvelis and Yu (1997) and Mausser and Laguna, whose method it extends 'from nearly two decades of improvements in MILO solvers and computers'; contrasts Assavapokee et al.'s three-level method and Iancu and Trichakis's Pareto-robust selection by a hand-picked scenario (pp. 3–4, 7, 9).
writing: Four-bullet contribution list (p. 3); a toy portfolio example where all RO solutions tie and the CR solution diversifies (p. 9); hedged recommendations ('suggest', 'should be considered') (pp. 19–20).
limits_future: Stated: convex Π handled only for the budget set; few intermediate Pareto solutions for integer problems (p. 9); cuts could be problem-specific (p. 11). Future: choose among Pareto solutions by simulation, back-testing and risk preferences (p. 20). [my reading] The intractability of the convex case is asserted (p. 19) from nonconvexity (pp. 6–7), without a hardness proof; the conclusion favours equal weights (p. 20) while §5.2 names λ = 0.6 (p. 14).

method_links.note: The regret and CR devices keep the nominal class (LO to LO, MILO to MILO) when Π is concave, and the boundary is printed: convex Π gives a nonconvex inner problem, handled only for the budget set.

An inherited tractability belief is re-measured (CR 10–20 times RO; regret as fast as RO), and the MILO route is said to benefit from two decades of solver and computer progress, but no figure is built.

One scalar knob λ blends two notions of robustness into a frontier, and a bad case is printed (the dense graph, where CR loses); no bound. The paper also offers an alternative to the Pareto-efficiency critique cited under Method 3's correction (Iancu–Trichakis, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2013.1753).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the absolute robust objective is divided by its own optimum ΠRO so that it is dimensionless like the competitive ratio before the two are weighted by λ; λ = ε then breaks ties among robust optima

transferable: For a regret objective whose clairvoyant LP is concave in the uncertainty, substitute the clairvoyant LP, merge the minimizations and dualize; the robust regret model needs one extra variable per set constraint and parameter (pp. 5–6).
For a bilinear inner problem over a budget set, restrict deviations to {−1, 0, 1} by the vertex theorem and linearize binary × bounded-continuous products exactly (pp. 7–8).
To break ties among robust optima, add an ε-weighted secondary objective instead of optimizing a hand-picked scenario (p. 9).
Judge robust solutions by simulated percentiles of both absolute and relative metrics, not only by the worst case (Figs. 3, 5, 8, 11–13, pp. 11–19).

quotes.text: However, over the past ten years the focus has primarily been on absolute worst-case objective functions, which have generally been considered to be more tractable.
This suggests that optimizing for a relative regret objective function is essentially no harder than optimizing for an absolute robust objective function in settings such as those considered here.

title: Computation of exact bootstrap confidence intervals: Complexity and deterministic algorithms
contribution: Recasts the exact bootstrap of the sample mean as counting integer points in a polyhedron, proves exact bootstrap quantiles (and the CDF of a sum of i.i.d. discrete variables) #P-hard, gives the first FPTAS and a simple exact algorithm by polynomial powers and Kronecker substitution, and shows on real and constructed data that randomized bootstrap intervals can err badly even at B = 1 million while the deterministic ones run in minutes for a few hundred points.
problem_entry: {ML (statistics)+IO} Practitioners compute the bootstrap by Monte Carlo, which only approximates the exact bootstrap; the randomization error can be large and invites reporting a lucky run; exact computation is believed intractable and existing exact methods cover n ≤ 9 or specific statistics (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: Bootstrap samples with mean ≤ α are the integer points of a polyhedron; reduce from #Knapsack for hardness, approximate the counting recursion on a geometric grid for an FPTAS, and compute all counts exactly as the coefficients of (Σ t^{z_i})ⁿ via one large-integer power (pp. 5–11).
assumptions: Positive integer data (m-bit data scaled by 2^m) (p. 7); the sample mean and additive statistics (1/n)Σf(z_i) (pp. 11–12); data: 124 Framingham patients on blood-pressure medication (p. 12), a constructed 81-point set (p. 13), random sets with n = 20–300 and z(n) up to 10⁵ (p. 14).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: reduction from equality #Knapsack with a large base M = 2n(n + 1)b and a counting identity (pp. 5–6)
Theorems 1–2: G(α) and H(β) #P-hard, the latter by binary search on the monotone H (pp. 6–7)
Corollary 1: the CDF of a sum of i.i.d. discrete variables is #P-hard (p. 7)
Lemmas 2–3: sandwich bounds by induction for the grid-rounded recursion give a (1 + ε)-factor approximation (p. 8)
Theorem 3: generating-function induction for the coefficients of (Σ t^{z_i})ⁿ (p. 10)
Proposition 1: Kronecker substitution with the tight coefficient bound nⁿ packs all coefficients into one integer (pp. 10–11)
Propositions A.1–A.2: a discontinuity in the exact distribution explains the randomized estimate's instability (pp. 15–16)
experiments: C++/MPFR for the FPTAS, Julia BigInt/GMP for the exact and randomized methods, LattE (Barvinok) as a further baseline; no machine named (p. 12). Framingham: 300 randomized runs with B = 100,000 vary strongly for small β while the exact and ε = 0.01 curves do not (pp. 12–13). Constructed data: exact H(0.025) ≈ 38.4, but with B = 1 million more than 25% of runs fall below 28 (p. 13); [my reading] the text says 200 runs and then 'the 100 runs'. FPTAS in minutes for n ≤ 300 at ε = 0.05; the exact algorithm fails from memory at z(n) = 10⁵ and n ≥ 150; LattE 466 s at n = 20, over an hour at n = 30 (pp. 14–15).
positioning: Joins the deterministic-over-randomized line (Bertsimas et al. 2015) to integer counting (Barvinok; Štefankovič et al. 2012 FPTAS for #Knapsack; Nesterov's polynomial method); prior exact bootstrap methods are for small n or specific statistics (pp. 3–5).
writing: The abstract opens with the belief and lists three advances; hardness is presented as underscoring the belief rather than overturning it (pp. 2, 5); a clinical-trial example motivates determinism (p. 3).
limits_future: Printed: the exact algorithm's memory limit at five significant digits (pp. 14–15); additive statistics only (p. 11). Future: deterministic algorithms for other resampling methods (p. 15).

method_links.note: A statistics quantity is written exactly in an OR class, but a counting class rather than LP, conic or MIO; the boundary is printed twice (#P-hardness; the exact algorithm's memory limit).
The intractability belief is not overturned but proved; practicality comes from an approximation with a guarantee at clinical-trial sizes, not from solver speed-ups.

The incumbent (randomized bootstrap at B = 10⁵ and 10⁶, run 300 and 200 times) is dueled on real and constructed data; every deterministic answer carries a guarantee; failures are printed (memory, LattE).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimization over randomization (Taste mark 3 as a Method)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Monte Carlo resampling is replaced by deterministic algorithms with guarantees; the paper cites the 2015 experimental-design paper as showing 'the power of deterministic methods over randomized methods'; S312 in this batch does the same for training splits

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: pathological instance for the randomized incumbent
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an 81-point data set whose exact distribution jumps across the 2.5% quantile makes the Monte Carlo estimate flip between about 27.5 and 38.4 even at B = 1 million

transferable: To show a resampling quantity is hard, encode resamples as integer points of a polyhedron and reduce from #Knapsack with a large-base digit construction (pp. 5–6).
To count sums of n draws, raise a generating polynomial to the n-th power and read all coefficients from one large-integer power by Kronecker substitution, using GMP (pp. 10–11).
To defeat a Monte Carlo incumbent at moderate quantiles, build data whose exact distribution jumps across the target quantile (p. 13; pp. 15–16).
Argue for determinism as a guard against reporting a lucky random run (pp. 3, 13).

quotes.text: Since calculating exact bootstrap quantities is believed to be intractable, randomized resampling algorithms are traditionally used.
As an additional benefit, the proposed deterministic algorithms remove the temptation of a practitioner to run the randomized algorithm many times until a desirable estimate is obtained.

title: Stochastic optimization in supply chain networks: averaging robust solutions
contribution: Treats the budget Γ of limit-law uncertainty sets as a random variable (half-normal, from a reflected-random-walk argument) and approximates expected supply-chain cost by a quadrature-weighted average of worst-case costs, which keeps the robust problem's class; a Bienstock–Özbay-style decomposition with MIO adversaries finds base-stock levels within about 1.3–4.7% (one case 9.4%) of the sample-average stochastic optimum in 2–4 iterations.
problem_entry: {RO+SD; IO as engine} Stochastic analysis of multi-echelon networks has closed forms only for simple systems, stochastic programming needs scenarios and simulation optimization needs gradient estimators, while RO needs a chosen Γ that is hard to match to average performance (pp. 4–5).
key_idea: Expected cost ≈ E_Γ[worst-case cost over U(Γ)], with Γ half-normal and discretized by quadrature; minimize Σ f_i q_i with epigraph constraints per Γ_i, the same class as single-Γ RO, by alternating a decision-maker problem and adversarial MIOs (pp. 8–12).
assumptions: Periodic review, backlogging, zero lead times, no seasonality, light-tailed demand (p. 6); normalized partial sums of demand bounded by Γ per echelon (Assumption 1, pp. 8–9); (s, S) policies (p. 12); means and SDs 'could be inferred from historical data' (p. 8); five synthetic networks with 1–9 installations and normal, lognormal, gamma or uniform demand (p. 13).
proof_devices: half-normal density for Γ from P(L ≤ L̂(Γ) | ω) = 2Φ(Γ) − 1 in a single-installation Lindley recursion with a reflected-Brownian approximation (eqs. 10–12, p. 9)
quadrature discretization of E_Γ (eq. 13, p. 9) and an epigraph reformulation in the class of the single-Γ problem (eqs. 15–16, p. 10)
Benders-style decomposition after Bienstock and Özbay (2008): working lists of adversarial demands, upper and lower bounds (pp. 11–12)
adversarial problem (non-concave) reformulated as an MIO with auxiliary variables (p. 12)
experiments: Against simulation (10,000 replications), one installation: 19.2%, 6.5% and 4.4% error at T = 1, 12 and 24 (p. 14). Against a sample-average stochastic solution: under 10% for σ = 10–100, while fixed Γ = 2 and 3 do worse (Fig. 4, p. 15); solution errors 1.3–4.7% over networks except 9.38% for instance (3) at T = 9 (Table 2, p. 16). 2–4 iterations, up to 1,527 s, with 2% bound and MIO gaps and a 120 s limit per MIO (Tables 2–3, p. 16); no solver or machine named. [my reading] Objective errors of 16.4–18.5% for the nine-installation network (Table 4, p. 17) are not discussed.
positioning: Continues the Bandi–Bertsimas robust-probability programme and Bandi, Bertsimas and Youssef's transient queueing work; builds on Bienstock and Özbay's (2008) robust base-stock algorithm; contrasts stochastic programming and simulation optimization (pp. 4–6, 11).
writing: A four-point list of what the approach avoids (dimension, scenarios, replications) (p. 6); the abstract announces three findings, one of which (affine policies) the manuscript does not report [my reading] (pp. 3, 12–17).
limits_future: Stated: accuracy relies on the central limit theorem and is better for long horizons (p. 14). [my reading] The promised affine-policy results and the Section 3.3 cited on p. 8 are absent; no convergence or error bound; synthetic networks only.

method_links.note: Averaging over Γ keeps the robust problem's class. title: Novel mixed integer optimization sparse regression approach in chemometrics
contribution: Brings ridge-regularized best-subset regression by MIO to LIBS calibration of mineral ores: on 52 reference materials it averages R² 0.88 with 4.3 variables, against 0.77–0.78 for glmnet and PLS and 805.8 variables for SPLS, keeps R² 0.69 under heavy synthetic noise where the others turn negative, and lets the selected emission lines be checked against physics.
problem_entry: {ML+IO; RO through the ridge term; AP} Chemometrics calibrates with PCA/PLS components that mix all variables or with L1 shrinkage; best subset was left to leaps and bounds (about 40 variables) and heuristics; MIO was 'regarded as intractable' but solver and hardware speed-ups now make it usable, and no chemometrics paper had used it (p. 2).
key_idea: min ‖Y − Xβ‖² + γ‖β‖² subject to ‖β‖₀ ≤ k, the ridge term read as robustness to bounded noise; solved by SubsetSelection's relaxation for thousands of variables and by big-M MIO below 100; k and γ by cross-validation (pp. 3–5).
assumptions: 52 OREAS certified reference materials measured by an Elemission LIBS system; 3,828 spectral variables; 10 elements including trace Li (pp. 4, 8); one random split of 40 training/validation and 12 test samples (pp. 4–5); synthetic Gaussian noise with the signal's covariance for robustness (p. 7).
proof_devices: no new theory: robust counterpart under ℓq-bounded noise equals a q*-norm penalty, cited from Bertsimas and Copenhaver (p. 3)
big-M and outer-approximation formulations of best subset reviewed (pp. 3–4)

[my reading] the introduction claims optimal solutions (p. 2), but full-spectrum fits use a relaxation (p. 4) that card S095 (c22) describes as a dual sub-gradient method for a Boolean relaxation; no gap is reported
experiments: Baselines glmnet (R), pls v2.7-1, SPLS with 30 restarts (p. 5). Average R² 0.88 (SMIO) against 0.78 (PLS), 0.77 (glmnet), 0.68 (SPLS); 4.3 variables against 16.1 and 805.8 (Table 2, pp. 5, 8); lowest test MSE for 5 of 10 elements, worst for K [my count, Table 1, p. 5]. Noise: R² 0.69 at the highest level while the others are negative (pp. 1, 8). Intel Core i7-8750H, 16 GB: under 2 min per fit on 3,828 variables, under 20 min for CV over 5 γ × 4 k; big-M could not run on full spectra (p. 8).
positioning: Against PCA/PLS, LASSO, sparse PCA and SPLS in chemometrics and against leaps-and-bounds and heuristic subset selection; claims the first MIO method in a chemometrics paper; leans on the group's sparse-regression algorithms (refs. 22, 33, 36) (pp. 2–4).
writing: Highlights and abstract lead with headline numbers (R², variables, noise); the 'why now' paragraph repeats the solver and hardware speed-up figures (p. 2); a worked example on K shows how interpretability guides the model (p. 7).
limits_future: Stated: two or three tuning parameters instead of one; longer run times; big-M fails under strong collinearity (p. 8). Future: bootstrapping, losses and penalties matched to the noise, classification, sparse PLS by MIO (p. 8). [my reading] One 12-sample test split; the fix for K is reported on test performance (p. 7).

method_links.note: The 'why now' carries a borrowed figure: solvers 1,250,000 times faster 1990–2016 and 'more than 2 trillion' with hardware, cited to Bixby, Gurobi and Nemhauser; the 2 trillion is the figure SKILL dates to 2018. Nothing is rebuilt for this class or machine (step 3 and its checkpoint).

Incumbents are dueled in their standard implementations on a stated machine, but at scale no certificate is given while the introduction claims optimality; this repeats the ⚠ already recorded under Method 4.
The robust counterpart under norm-bounded noise is a penalized problem, so robustness costs no class change (Heuristic 1: the robust problem behind regularization).
The programme enters a new field through a student, an instrument maker and an industrial funder, with Bertsimas credited for supervision and review.

title: The edge of optimization in large-scale vehicle routing for paratransit
contribution: A cluster-then-route method for paratransit dial-a-ride at city scale: iterated matching on a shareability graph with exact DARPs on merged pairs, then an MIO that connects trips into driver itineraries under labor constraints with outsourcing; on a week of Boston's The RIDE data (3,000–7,400 requests a day) it raises productivity 30–40% over an insertion heuristic in under 20 minutes, and re-optimization after 20% cancellations cuts the productivity loss from 20% to about 5%.
problem_entry: {AP+IO; HS} ADA paratransit is costly (Access-a-Ride $472 million in 2015 with 4% from fares; The RIDE over $100 million with 6%); research has not reached practice because of simplified models, black boxes and scalability; exact DARP methods stop at hundreds of requests, and a plan must run in half an hour (pp. 2–4, 17).
key_idea: Shareability graph by enumerating the four ways to serve a pair, maximum-weight matching, then repeated condensation and re-matching with exact DARPs solved on each merged pair, warm-started by the previous trips; an MIO (TCP-Labor) connects trips with vehicle-provider indices, aggregated shifts, availability and outsourcing (pp. 9–16).
assumptions: The RIDE data, August–September 2018, evaluated on 10–16 September; 298–616 vehicles a day, shifts of 4–12 hours, 20- and 40-minute windows, ride time capped at 30 minutes over a direct taxi; conservative speeds advised by The RIDE (pp. 16, 18). Admitted simplifications: shareability weights computed once, nearest-neighbour pruning of connections, aggregated shifts with set-cover postprocessing, a stylized re-optimization (pp. 11, 15–16, 22–23, 26).
proof_devices: DARP formulation PDPTW1 with big-M linearization, found faster than the cutting-plane PDPTW2 on these data (pp. 7–8)
four-way enumeration of shared pairs and maximum-weight matching, then condensation into supernodes and re-matching (pp. 9–11)
warm starts for each small exact DARP from the previous iteration's trips (pp. 10–11, 22)
TCP-Labor MIO with vehicle type-provider index, time-indexed availability and outsourcing variables (eq. 6, pp. 14–15); set cover over sub-itineraries for shift feasibility (pp. 15–16)
gaps computed by enumeration on sparsified instances because solver gaps were loose (p. 19)
experiments: Julia, JuMP, Gurobi 8.1; enumeration on a Xeon cluster, other runs on an i7-6500U laptop with 16 GB (pp. 18–19). Random subsets of 50–1,600 requests: gaps 0.2–0.5% up to N = 200 against 1.3–4.3% (Santi) and 0.8–2.6% (OR-Tools); at N = 1,600, 10.4% and 19.6% better, OR-Tools capped at about three times this method's time (Table 2, pp. 19–21). Real week: productivity +30–40% over an insertion heuristic and +6–11% over Santi clusters, outsourcing 7.4% against 7.6% and 10.8%, under 20 min on weekdays, trip-connection gaps at most 0.03% under a 5-minute limit (Tables 5–6, pp. 23–26). Cancellations: productivity loss from 20% to about 5% (Table 7, pp. 26–27). [my reading] Utilization is lower than the heuristic's (Table 5, p. 24) and is not discussed.
positioning: Between metaheuristics that need tuning (tabu, insertion, LNS) and exact methods limited to hundreds of requests; extends Santi et al.'s shareability matching to higher capacity, against Alonso-Mora et al.'s clique enumeration, which blew up on these data (pp. 4–5, 11).
writing: Opens with costs and an impact gap; the title reuses the 'edge of optimization' brand; claims the largest DARP application in the literature and a method that 'requires no tuning' (pp. 1–3, 20).
limits_future: Stated: stale shareability weights (p. 11), pruning (p. 23), OR-Tools might improve with tuning (p. 20), the baseline is a proxy for The RIDE's unknown algorithm (p. 18), a stylized re-optimization (p. 26). Future: re-optimization for traffic and breakdowns; parallelization (pp. 25, 27). No deployment is reported.

method_links.note: The owner's metric (productivity per revenue hour) and operating rules frame the study, but the current rule is unknown, so a published insertion heuristic whose metrics match those The RIDE reports stands in for it; no field test.

Exact DARPs warm-started by the previous iteration; gaps measured by enumeration where possible and omitted, not guessed, for N ≥ 400; solver gaps and limits printed; incumbents dueled under a time cap. Heuristic 3: the full DARP stalls (loose Gurobi gaps even on small sizes), so MIO is kept for small pieces.
Solver progress 'in recent years' motivates the work, with no figure.
The 'edge of optimization' brand of the 2019 taxi-dispatch paper is reused with a new student and data partner (Heuristic 9).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: iterated matching-and-merge with warm-started exact subproblems
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a matching on a pairwise compatibility graph merges requests into trips; merged trips become supernodes that are re-matched, and an exact DARP is re-solved only on each matched pair, warm-started from the previous level, for up to 15 iterations

transferable: Grow exact subproblems gradually: match, merge matched pairs into supernodes, and re-solve the exact MIO only on each merged pair, warm-started from the previous level (pp. 10–11, 22).
When the operator's algorithm is unknown, implement the published method most likely in use and check its metrics against the operator's reports before calling it the baseline (p. 18).
Compute optimality gaps by enumeration on sparsified small instances when solver gaps are loose, and state the sizes for which no gap exists (p. 19; Table 2, p. 21).
Re-plan after disruptions by shrinking time windows around the promises already made and rerunning the whole pipeline (p. 25).

quotes.text: We do not know the details of the algorithm that The RIDE currently uses for its operations.

We chose to compute the gaps through enumeration rather than solving a MIO problem since the gaps from Gurobi could be quite large even on small problem sizes, possibly because of the lazy constraints (1d).
